slides.title: What is money?
slides.text:
Money is a tool people use to pay for things. Instead of trading a toy for a sandwich, we can use money so everyone knows what something costs.

Example: If you have $5, you might spend $2 on a snack and still have $3 left to save for later.

widgetConfig.scenario: Instead of trading a toy directly for a sandwich, you use something else to pay for it. What is this tool called?

options.label: Money
options.outcome: Exactly right! Money is a tool people use to pay for things, instead of trading a toy directly for a sandwich.

options.label: A barter
options.outcome: A barter is trading items directly — using a tool to pay instead is what money does.

options.label: A gift
options.outcome: A gift is given for free — paying for something with a tool like this is called money.

slides.title: How can people get money?
slides.text:
People usually get money by earning it, receiving it as a gift, or sometimes getting an allowance. Earning means doing work or helping with a job.

Example: You might earn $2 for helping wash the car, while a grown-up earns money by doing their job.

widgetConfig.scenario: You help wash the car and earn $2. What is this an example of?

options.label: Earning money by doing work
options.outcome: Exactly right! People usually get money by earning it through work, like helping wash the car.

options.label: Money appearing with no effort
options.outcome: Money didn't just appear — you earned it by doing the work of washing the car.

options.label: This is not a way people get money
options.outcome: This actually is a common way people get money — earning it by doing work.

slides.title: What are coins and bills?
slides.text:
Coins and bills are two forms of money you can hold in your hand. Different coins and bills have different values.

Example: Four quarters equal $1, and a $5 bill is worth the same as five $1 bills.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have a jar of coins and a $5 bill. What are both of these?

options.label: Two forms of money you can hold in your hand
options.outcome: Exactly right! Coins and bills are both physical forms of money, just in different shapes and values.

options.label: Coins are money but bills are just paper
options.outcome: Bills are real money too, just like coins — both are forms of money you can hold.

options.label: Only bills count as real money
options.outcome: Coins count as real money too — both coins and bills are forms of money.

slides.title: What does spending mean?
slides.text:
Spending means using some of your money to buy something. After you spend it, that money is no longer available for another purchase.

Example: If you have $6 and spend $2 on a snack, you have $4 left.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have $6 and spend $2 on a snack. How much do you have left?

options.outcome: Exactly right! Spending $2 from $6 leaves you with $4.

options.label: $6, since spending does not change your money
options.outcome: Spending does change how much you have — $6 minus $2 leaves $4, not $6.
Spending reduces your money, it doesn't increase it — $6 minus $2 leaves $4.

slides.title: What is a store?
slides.text:
A store is a place where people can buy things. Stores put prices on items so you know how much money you need.

Example: If a book costs $8 and you have $10, you can buy it and have $2 left.

widgetConfig.scenario: A book costs $8 and you have $10. What happens if you buy it?

options.label: You have $2 left
options.outcome: Exactly right! Stores put prices on items, and $10 minus the $8 book leaves you with $2.

options.label: You have $10 left, since prices do not matter
options.outcome: Prices do matter — buying the $8 book from your $10 leaves you with $2, not $10.

options.label: You cannot buy it since stores do not have prices
options.outcome: Stores do have prices — that's exactly how you know the book costs $8.

slides.title: What does sharing money mean?
slides.text:
Sharing money means choosing to use some of it to help or make someone else happy. You can give to a person, buy a gift, or donate to a cause.

Example: If you have $5, you might save $4 and use $1 to help an animal shelter.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have 4 stickers and your friend has none. What's a kind thing you could do?

options.label: Share a couple of your stickers with your friend
options.outcome: That's so kind! Sharing what you have can make everyone happy.

options.label: Keep them all and don't share
options.outcome: That's okay sometimes, but sharing can be a kind way to make a friend happy too.

options.label: Take your friend's things instead
options.outcome: Taking things isn't sharing — sharing means giving some of what's yours, not taking from others.

slides.title: What choices can you make with money?
slides.text:
Money gives you choices. You can spend some now, save some for later, and share some with others.

Example: From $10, you might spend $3, save $5, and share $2.

widgetConfig.scenario: From $10, you spend $3, save $5, and share $2. What does this show?

options.label: Money gives you choices, like spending, saving, and sharing
options.outcome: Exactly right! Money gives you choices — you can spend some now, save some for later, and share some with others.

options.label: Money can only ever be spent, never saved or shared
options.outcome: Money can actually be saved or shared too, not just spent — this example splits it three ways.

options.label: You must always spend all your money at once
options.outcome: You don't have to spend it all at once — money gives you the choice to save and share too.

slides.title: How can work help you earn money?
slides.text:
Work means using your time and effort to do something useful. Sometimes people are paid for that work.

Example: You might earn money for helping rake leaves, while a teacher earns money for teaching students.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want more money for a toy. What's a way to earn it rather than just asking for it?

options.label: Do extra chores or small jobs to earn it
options.outcome: Exactly! Doing work, like chores, is a great way to earn money instead of just asking for it.

options.label: Just wait for money to appear
options.outcome: Money doesn't just appear — doing some kind of work or chores is how you earn it.

options.label: Take money without asking
options.outcome: Taking money isn't earning it — doing chores or small jobs is the right way to earn money.

slides.title: Does money really grow on trees?
slides.text:
No. The saying “money does not grow on trees” reminds us that money usually comes from work, saving, or gifts, so we should think before spending it.

Example: If you spend all $10 today, you will need to earn or receive more before you can buy something tomorrow.

widgetConfig.scenario: You spend all $10 today. Will more money just appear tomorrow?

options.label: No — you'll need to earn or receive more first
options.outcome: Exactly right! Money does not grow on trees — you need to earn, save, or receive more before you can buy something tomorrow.

options.label: Yes, money always grows back on its own
options.outcome: Money doesn't grow back on its own — you need to earn or receive more first.

options.label: Money grows on trees just like fruit
options.outcome: Money doesn't grow on trees — it usually comes from work, saving, or gifts.

slides.title: What does saving mean?
slides.text:
Saving means keeping some money for later instead of spending it all now. Saving helps you be ready for something you want in the future.

Example: If you get $5 and save $2, you still have that $2 for another day.

widgetConfig.scenario: You get $5 and save $2 instead of spending it all. What does this let you do?

options.label: Keep that $2 for something later
options.outcome: Exactly right! Saving means keeping some money for later instead of spending it all now.

options.label: Lose the $2 completely
options.outcome: Saving doesn't mean losing it — you keep that $2 for something you want later.

options.label: Saving means spending more than you have
options.outcome: Saving is actually the opposite — it means keeping some money instead of spending it all.

slides.title: How can your savings grow?
slides.text:
Your savings grow when you keep adding money instead of using it all. Even small amounts can become a bigger amount over time.

Example: Saving $1 each week gives you $4 after four weeks.

widgetConfig.scenario: You keep putting a little money into your savings jar every week instead of spending it all. What happens over time?

options.label: Your savings grow bigger
options.outcome: Exactly right! Your savings grow when you keep adding money instead of using it all.

options.label: Your savings shrink on their own
options.outcome: Savings don't shrink on their own — adding money regularly makes them grow.

options.label: Savings never change no matter what you do
options.outcome: Savings do change — adding a little regularly is exactly what makes them grow over time.

slides.title: What does a bank do?
slides.text:
A bank is a place that can keep money in an account and keep track of how much belongs to you. Adults often use banks instead of keeping all their cash at home.

Example: If you put $20 into a bank account, the bank records that $20 as part of your balance.

widgetConfig.scenario: You put $20 into a bank account. What does the bank do with it?

options.label: Keeps it safe and tracks that it belongs to you
options.outcome: Exactly right! A bank keeps money in an account and keeps track of how much belongs to you.

options.label: Keeps the money for itself with no record
options.outcome: A bank doesn't keep your money for itself — it tracks that the $20 belongs to you.

options.label: Banks never keep track of how much is yours
options.outcome: Banks actually do keep track of your balance — that's one of their main jobs.

slides.title: Can a bank pay you for saving?
slides.text:
Some bank accounts pay a small amount called interest. Interest is extra money the bank adds based on how much money is in the account.

Example: Your $20 might become a little more than $20 over time because of interest.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your $20 sits in a bank account for a while. Could it become a little more than $20?

options.label: Yes — through interest the bank adds
options.outcome: Exactly right! Some bank accounts pay interest, extra money the bank adds based on how much is in the account.

options.label: No, bank balances never change on their own
options.outcome: Bank balances can actually grow a little through interest, which the bank adds over time.

options.label: Banks only ever take money away, never add it
options.outcome: Banks can actually add money through interest, not just hold or take it away.

slides.title: How can money be for now and later?
slides.text:
You do not have to choose between spending everything and saving everything. You can use some money now and keep some for later.

Example: From $6, you might spend $2 today and save $4 for a bigger goal.

widgetConfig.scenario: From $6, you spend $2 today and save $4. Do you have to choose between spending everything or saving everything?

options.label: No — you can do both at once
options.outcome: Exactly right! You do not have to choose between spending everything and saving everything — you can use some now and keep some for later.

options.label: Yes, you must pick only one or the other
options.outcome: You don't have to pick only one — you can spend some and save some at the same time.

options.label: Saving some and spending some is never possible
options.outcome: Saving some and spending some is actually very possible, and a smart way to use money.

slides.title: Why save for something special?
slides.text:
Some things cost more than the money you have today. Saving lets you collect money little by little until you have enough.

Example: A toy costs $12. If you save $3 each week, you can reach $12 in four weeks.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want a big toy that costs more than you have right now. What can help you get it?

options.label: Save a little bit at a time until you have enough
options.outcome: Exactly! Saving a little at a time adds up until you can afford the big toy.

options.label: Give up since you don't have enough today
options.outcome: You don't have to give up — saving a little over time can get you there!

options.label: Take it without paying
options.outcome: That's not okay — saving up until you can pay for it is the right way.

slides.title: What is a savings goal?
slides.text:
A savings goal is something specific you are saving money for. Knowing your goal can make it easier to keep saving.

Example: Write “$15 art set” on a jar and add money until the jar reaches $15.

widgetConfig.scenario: You decide you want to save up exactly $20 for a new game. What is this target called?

options.label: A savings goal
options.outcome: Exactly right! A savings goal is the specific amount you're aiming to save for something you want.

options.label: A spending limit
options.outcome: A spending limit is different — a savings goal is specifically the target amount you're trying to save toward.

options.label: An allowance
options.outcome: An allowance is regular money you receive — a savings goal is the specific target you're saving up toward.

slides.title: Why should you count your savings?
slides.text:
Counting your savings shows how close you are to your goal. It also helps you notice that small amounts really add up.

Example: $3 this week plus $2 next week gives you $5 total.

widgetConfig.scenario: You saved $3 this week and $2 next week. Why is counting this useful?

options.label: It shows you have $5 total and how close you are to your goal
options.outcome: Exactly right! Counting your savings shows how close you are to your goal and helps you notice that small amounts really add up.

options.label: Counting savings never tells you anything
options.outcome: Counting savings actually tells you a lot — like how close you are to your goal.

options.label: Small amounts never add up to anything
options.outcome: Small amounts actually do add up — $3 plus $2 already gives you $5 toward your goal.

slides.title: Why can waiting be a smart money choice?
slides.text:
Waiting gives you time to save more and decide whether you still want something. Sometimes you discover that a bigger goal matters more than a quick purchase.

Example: Skipping a $2 treat four times could leave you with $8 toward a game.

widgetConfig.scenario: You skip a $2 treat four times. What could this leave you with toward a game?

options.label: $8 saved toward the game
options.outcome: Exactly right! Waiting gives you time to save more — skipping a $2 treat four times could leave you with $8 toward your game.

options.label: Nothing, since skipping treats never adds up
options.outcome: Skipping treats actually does add up — four $2 treats skipped equals $8 saved.

options.label: Waiting is never a smart choice with money
options.outcome: Waiting can actually be a smart money choice — it gives you time to save more toward something bigger.

slides.title: What is a bank?
slides.text:
A bank is a business that keeps money in accounts, helps people send and receive money, and may pay interest on savings. Your account balance shows how much money belongs to you.

Example: If you deposit $25 and later spend $5, your balance would be about $20, not counting any interest or fees.

widgetConfig.scenario: A bank keeps money in accounts and helps people send and receive money. What kind of place is a bank?

options.label: A business that keeps money safe and helps manage it
options.outcome: Exactly right! A bank is a business that keeps money in accounts, helps people send and receive money, and keeps it safe.

options.label: A place that only gives away free money
options.outcome: A bank isn't about giving away free money — it's a business that safely keeps and manages money.

options.label: A place where money disappears forever once you put it in
options.outcome: Money doesn't disappear in a bank — it stays yours, safely kept and tracked in your account.

slides.title: How do you save for a goal?
slides.text:
Start by choosing what you want, finding its price, and deciding how much you can save regularly. Breaking a big price into smaller steps makes the goal easier to reach.

Example: A $60 bike could be reached by saving $5 a week for 12 weeks.

widgetConfig.prompt: Tap the steps in the right order
items: Decide how much to save regularly

slides.title: What is interest?
slides.text:
Interest is money paid for the use of money. A bank may pay you interest for keeping savings there, while a borrower may pay interest when using someone else’s money.

Example: If your savings earn interest, your balance can slowly become larger even if you do not add more money.

widgetConfig.scenario: You put $10 in a savings account, and a year later it's $10.50. What happened?

options.label: The bank paid you interest for keeping your money there
options.outcome: Exactly! Interest is extra money the bank pays you for saving with them.

options.label: The bank made a mistake
options.outcome: That's not a mistake — banks pay interest as a reward for keeping your savings with them.

options.label: Money randomly grows in bank accounts
options.outcome: It's not random — it's interest, a small percentage the bank pays you for saving there.

slides.title: What is the difference between a need and a want?
slides.text:
A need is something important for living or staying safe, such as food, basic clothing, or a home. A want is something enjoyable but not necessary.

Example: A winter coat when it is freezing can be a need; a second fancy jacket may be a want.

slides.title: What is a budget?
slides.text:
A budget is a plan for how you will use your money before you spend it. It can include money for spending, saving, and sharing.

Example: If you have $20, you might plan $8 for spending, $10 for saving, and $2 for sharing.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have $20 and plan $8 for spending, $10 for saving, $2 for sharing. What is this plan called?

options.label: A budget
options.outcome: Exactly right! A budget is a plan for how you will use your money before you spend it.

options.label: A receipt
options.outcome: A receipt records what you already bought — a plan made before spending is called a budget.

options.label: This has no name
options.outcome: This kind of plan actually has a name — it's called a budget.

slides.title: Why can waiting before buying help?
slides.text:
Waiting gives you time to compare choices, save more, and decide whether you really want the item. This can prevent impulse purchases.

Example: Before spending $15 on a toy today, you might wait two days and decide you would rather put the $15 toward a $40 game.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're about to spend $15 on a toy. What could waiting two days help you do?

options.label: Decide if you'd rather save it toward something bigger
options.outcome: Exactly right! Waiting gives you time to compare choices, save more, and decide whether you really want the item, which can prevent impulse purchases.

options.label: Nothing — waiting never changes your decision
options.outcome: Waiting actually can change your decision — it gives you time to think about what you really want.

options.label: Waiting always means you can never buy it later
options.outcome: Waiting doesn't mean you can never buy it — it just gives you time to decide if you still want it.

slides.title: Why should you compare prices?
slides.text:
The same or similar item can cost different amounts at different stores. Comparing prices helps you keep more of your money.

Example: If headphones cost $25 in one place and $19 somewhere else, comparing first could save you $6.

widgetConfig.scenario: Headphones cost $25 in one place and $19 elsewhere. What could comparing save you?

options.outcome: Exactly right! Comparing prices here could save you $6, since the same item costs different amounts at different stores.

options.label: Nothing — prices are always the same everywhere
options.outcome: Prices actually can differ between stores — comparing them here could save you $6.
That's the higher price, not the amount you'd save — comparing could save you the $6 difference.

slides.title: How do you set a savings goal?
slides.text:
Choose a clear target, write down the amount, and decide how often you will save. Then track your progress.

Example: To save $24 in eight weeks, you could aim to save $3 each week.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to save $24 in eight weeks. How much should you aim to save each week?

options.label: $3 each week
options.outcome: Exactly right! Choosing a clear target and deciding how often to save, like $3 each week, helps you reach $24 in eight weeks.

options.label: $24 all at once with no weekly plan
options.outcome: A weekly plan, like $3 a week, makes an $24 goal much easier to track than trying to save it all at once.

options.label: Savings goals never need a clear target
options.outcome: Savings goals actually work much better with a clear target and a plan for how often to save.

slides.title: Why track what you spend?
slides.text:
Writing down purchases helps you see where your money goes. Small purchases can be easy to forget, but together they can use a large part of your money.

Example: Three $3 snacks in a week cost $9 altogether.

widgetConfig.scenario: Three $3 snacks in a week. How much do they cost altogether?

options.outcome: Exactly right! Writing down purchases helps you see that three $3 snacks add up to $9 altogether.

options.label: $3, since only one snack really counts
options.outcome: All three snacks count toward your spending — together they add up to $9, not just $3.

options.label: Tracking spending never reveals anything useful
options.outcome: Tracking spending actually reveals a lot — like how small purchases such as these snacks add up to $9.

quiz.question: What is a bank?

A place that takes your money away
quiz.explanation: A bank keeps your money safe, like a giant piggy bank that tracks every dollar. Some banks even pay you extra just for saving there.

quiz.question: If a bank gives you a little extra money just for saving, what's that called?

Interest

quiz.question: Which one is a "need"?

Food
quiz.explanation: A need is something you must have to live, like food, water, or clothes. A want, like a new video game, is nice but not required.

quiz.question: A bike costs $60 and you save $5 a week. About how many weeks until you can afford it?
choices: About 12 weeks
It can never be saved for
quiz.explanation: Saving $5 every week adds up: after 12 weeks, you'll have $60 for the bike. Breaking a big goal into small weekly steps makes it easier to reach.

quiz.question: What's it called when you plan out ahead of time how you'll use your money?

A trophy

quiz.question: What can help make a savings goal feel more real?
choices: Picking one specific thing to save for
Never deciding what you're saving for

quiz.question: What's the difference between a "want" and a "need"?
choices: A need is required, a want is nice to have
They mean exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: A need is something you must have, like food or a coat in winter. A want, like a new toy, is nice to have but not necessary.

quiz.question: Why is it helpful to write down what you spend?
choices: It helps you see where your money is going
It makes your money disappear
quiz.explanation: Writing down what you buy shows exactly where your money goes each week. Small purchases, like a $2 snack a few times, can quietly add up to a lot.

quiz.question: You wait two weeks instead of buying a toy right away, and end up affording a better one. What does that show?
choices: Patience can pay off
Waiting never helps
quiz.explanation: Waiting before buying gives you time to save more and sometimes afford something better. Skipping a small toy today could mean a bigger one in just a couple of weeks.

slides.title: What is a bank account?
slides.text:
A bank account is a record the bank keeps of your money. It shows deposits, withdrawals, purchases, and your current balance.

Example: If your account has $30 and you deposit $10, the balance becomes $40 before any other activity.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your account has $30 and you deposit $10. What's your new balance?

options.outcome: Exactly right! A bank account records deposits and withdrawals — $30 plus a $10 deposit gives you a $40 balance.

options.label: $30, since deposits do not change the balance
options.outcome: Deposits do change the balance — adding $10 to $30 gives you $40.
That's just the deposit amount, not your new total — $30 plus $10 gives you $40.

slides.title: How can you watch your savings grow?
slides.text:
Track the amount you save each week or month. Seeing the total increase can show how repeated small choices build a bigger result.

Example: Saving $3 each week could look like $3, $6, $9, and $12 after four weeks.

widgetConfig.scenario: You save $3 each week. What would the total look like after four weeks?

options.outcome: Exactly right! Tracking the amount you save each week shows the total increasing — $3, $6, $9, and $12 after four weeks.

options.label: $3 every single week with no growth

options.label: Watching savings grow never shows anything useful
options.outcome: Watching savings grow actually shows something useful — how repeated small choices build a bigger result.

slides.title: What do risk and reward mean?
slides.text:
Risk is the chance that an investment may lose value. Reward is the chance that it may gain value. Investments with more possible growth often also come with more uncertainty.

Example: $20 invested might become $23, but it could also fall to $17 for a while—or even lose more.

slides.title: Why not put all your money in one investment?
slides.text:
If all your money is in one company and that company has trouble, your whole investment can be hurt. Spreading money across different investments is called diversification.

Example: Owning small pieces of many companies means one company doing badly has a smaller effect on everything you own.

slides.title: How is saving different from investing?
slides.text:
Saving is usually for money you want to keep easy to reach and relatively stable. Investing means accepting some risk in hopes that your money grows over a longer time.

Example: Money for a birthday gift next month might stay in savings; money for a goal many years away might be invested.

slides.title: What is compound growth?
slides.text:
Compound growth happens when money you have already earned can also earn more money. Over time, growth can build on earlier growth.

Example: If $100 grows to $105, future growth can happen on $105, not only on the original $100.

slides.title: What is a stock?
slides.text:
A stock represents a small ownership share in a company. If you own a share, you own a tiny part of that business.

Example: Buying one share of a company means you become one of many owners, even though your piece may be very small.

options.label: An employee of the company

options.label: A customer with no ownership at all
options.outcome: Owning a share is more than being a customer — it gives you a small ownership stake in the business.

slides.title: Can familiar companies have stocks?
slides.text:
Many large companies that make phones, shoes, games, food, or other products are publicly traded, which means investors can buy shares in them. Not every company is public, though.

Example: A brand you know from a store might be owned by a public company whose shares trade in the stock market.

options.label: Only unknown companies can have stocks
options.outcome: It's actually the opposite in many cases — plenty of well-known, familiar companies are publicly traded too.

slides.title: Why does starting young matter?
slides.text:
Starting young gives money more time to potentially grow and compound. Time does not guarantee a profit, but it gives long-term investing more years to work.

Example: Money invested at age 10 has many more years to grow than money first invested at age 30.

options.label: Money invested at age 10
options.outcome: Exactly right! Starting young gives money more time to potentially grow and compound than money invested later.

options.label: Money invested at age 30
options.outcome: Money invested later has fewer years to grow — starting younger gives it more time to potentially compound.

options.label: Starting age never affects how long money can grow
options.outcome: Starting age actually affects this a lot — the younger you start, the more years your money has to potentially grow.

slides.title: Do investments go up and down?
slides.text:
Yes. Investment prices can rise and fall, sometimes quickly. A lower price does not guarantee it will recover, so investors think about risk, diversification, and how long they can leave the money invested.

Example: An investment worth $50 today might be worth $45 next month and $55 later—or it could stay lower.

options.label: Yes, investments always bounce back eventually
options.outcome: Investments don't always bounce back — a lower price doesn't guarantee recovery.

options.label: Investment prices never change at all
options.outcome: Investment prices actually can change quite a bit, sometimes quickly, rising and falling over time.

quiz.question: What is a bank account?
choices: A way the bank keeps track of exactly how much money you have
A type of toy
quiz.explanation: A bank account is like a digital piggy bank that keeps track of your exact balance. Instead of counting coins, you just check a number, like balance: $37.

quiz.question: Why is it helpful to write down and add up your savings each week?
choices: You can actually see your money growing toward your goal
It has no real purpose
quiz.explanation: Writing down your savings each week lets you actually watch the total climb, like $2, then $4, then $6. Seeing the numbers grow keeps you motivated to keep going.

quiz.question: What happens when you take a risk with your money?
choices: It could grow, but it could also lose value
Nothing ever changes
quiz.explanation: Taking a risk with money means it could grow bigger, but it could also shrink for a while. That up-and-down chance is part of how investing can earn more over time.

quiz.question: What does it mean to diversify your money?
choices: Spread it across a few different things
Put it all in one place
quiz.explanation: Diversifying means putting your money into a few different things instead of just one. If one investment does poorly, the others can help balance it out.

quiz.question: What is compound growth?
choices: When your interest earns its own interest too
When a bank charges you a fee
quiz.explanation: Compound growth happens when the interest you already earned starts earning its own interest too. Money left in the bank grows a little faster each year instead of staying flat.

quiz.question: What is a stock?
choices: A tiny piece of a company you can own
A type of bank account
quiz.explanation: A stock is a tiny piece of a real company that you can own. If that company sells more toys or games, your tiny piece can become worth more.

quiz.question: Can a company do well while its stock price still falls?
choices: Yes, because stock prices also depend on expectations and what buyers will pay
No, a successful company’s stock must always rise
quiz.explanation: Yes. Strong business results can help, but stock prices also reflect expectations, news, interest rates, competition, and what investors think will happen next.

quiz.question: Why does starting to save or invest young help so much?
choices: Your money has more time to grow
It doesn't make any difference
quiz.explanation: Starting to save or invest young gives your money many more years to grow. A few dollars saved at age 8 has far more time to add up than money started at 20.

quiz.question: An investment goes up some weeks and down other weeks. Is that normal?
choices: Yes, that's a normal part of investing
No, real investments never change
quiz.explanation: Yes. Investment prices naturally move up and down. A decline may recover, but it may also last or worsen, which is why investors use diversification and match risk to their time horizon.

quiz.question: What's the main difference between saving and investing?
choices: Saving focuses on stability and access; investing accepts more risk for possible long-term growth
They are exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: Saving is generally used for money that should stay accessible and relatively stable. Investing takes on market risk in hopes of growing money over a longer period.

slides.title: What is investing?
slides.text:
Investing means putting money into an asset—such as a stock or fund—with the goal of growing its value or earning income over time. Unlike saving, investing can lose value.

Example: You might invest $50 in a fund that owns many companies. Years later it could be worth more than $50, but there is no guarantee.

options.label: Yes, invested money always grows with no risk

options.label: Investing and saving are exactly the same thing

slides.title: What is a stock?
slides.text:
A stock is a unit of ownership in a company. When you buy shares, you become one of the company’s owners, although your percentage may be tiny.

Example: If a company has millions of shares, owning one share still gives you a very small ownership stake.

options.label: An owner only if you buy all the shares

slides.title: How are risk and reward connected?
slides.text:
Investors usually expect a possibility of higher return only when they are willing to accept some risk. Risk includes losing part—or in some cases all—of the money invested.

Example: A stock may offer more growth potential than cash savings, but its price can also fall sharply.

slides.title: What is an investment loss?
slides.text:
A loss means an investment is worth less than what you paid for it. If you sell, the loss becomes realized; if you keep holding, the value can still change up or down.

Example: If you buy at $100 and the value falls to $80, you are down $20 at that moment. It might recover, fall further, or stay near $80.

options.label: A permanent, final loss with no chance of change

options.label: Not really a loss until it falls to zero
options.outcome: A loss is already real at $80 compared to your $100 purchase — it doesn't need to reach zero to count.

slides.title: How is investing different from an allowance?
slides.text:
An allowance is money you receive. Investing is a choice you make with money you already have, putting it into an asset that may change in value.

Example: You might receive a $10 allowance, spend $5, save $3, and invest $2 with a parent’s help.

options.label: An allowance is money you receive; investing is a choice you make with money you have

options.label: They are exactly the same thing

options.label: Investing is just another word for receiving an allowance

slides.title: What is a company?
slides.text:
A company is an organization that sells products or services. Companies use money to pay workers, make products, advertise, build technology, and try to earn a profit.

Example: A game company might pay designers to create a game and then earn money when customers buy it.

options.label: A government

slides.title: Who can be an investor?
slides.text:
Investors can be ordinary people, retirement savers, businesses, or large institutions. Young people can learn about investing and, with an adult, may be able to invest through accounts designed for minors.

Example: A teenager might own a small amount of an index fund in a custodial account managed by a parent.

options.label: Investing is only for large institutions, never individuals

slides.title: Why can a stock price rise or fall?
slides.text:
Stock prices change because buyers and sellers disagree about what a company is worth. Earnings, growth expectations, competition, news, interest rates, and the overall economy can all matter.

Example: Strong sales may help a stock, but the price could still fall if investors expected even better results.

widgetConfig.scenario: A company has strong sales, but its stock price still falls. Why might this happen?

options.label: Investors expected even better results than what happened
options.outcome: Exactly right! Stock prices change because buyers and sellers disagree about what a company is worth — strong sales may still disappoint if investors expected even better results.

options.label: Stock prices never change for any reason
options.outcome: Stock prices actually change for many reasons, including whether results meet, beat, or fall short of what investors expected.

options.label: Strong sales always guarantee a rising price
options.outcome: Strong sales don't always guarantee a rising price — if investors expected even better results, the price could still fall.

slides.title: How is investing different from gambling?
slides.text:
Both investing and gambling involve risk, but they are not the same activity. Investing usually means buying an asset with an expected long-term economic value; gambling usually depends on a wager whose outcome is designed around chance.

Example: Buying a diversified fund is ownership in many businesses, while betting on a coin flip does not create ownership in an asset.

options.label: They're exactly the same thing
options.outcome: They're different — investing involves real ownership in businesses, while gambling is based on chance with no underlying asset.

options.label: Investing has zero risk unlike gambling

quiz.question: What does "investing" mean?
choices: Using money to buy something that can grow in value
Hiding money so nobody can find it
quiz.explanation: Investing means putting your money into something, like a small piece of a company, instead of just spending it. If that company grows, like a sneaker brand selling more shoes, your $50 piece could grow to $60 or more over time.

quiz.question: What is a stock?
choices: A type of bank account
A small piece of ownership in a company
quiz.explanation: A stock is a small piece of ownership in a real company, not just a fake certificate. If a video game company splits itself into 1,000 stocks and you own 1, you technically own 1/1000th of that whole business.

quiz.question: True or False: Investments only ever go up in value.
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation: False — investments can go up and down in value, not just rise forever. For example, $100 might grow to $110 in a good year but dip to $90 in a rough one before recovering; that ride is the risk that makes bigger rewards possible.

quiz.question: If a company you own a tiny piece of grows and does well, what usually happens to your piece?
choices: It becomes worth more
It disappears
quiz.explanation: When a company grows and earns more money, the small pieces of it that people own — including yours — usually become worth more too. It's like owning a slice of a pizza that keeps getting bigger.

quiz.question: An investment falls from $100 to $80. What is true before you sell it?
choices: Its market value is $20 lower, but the price can still move up or down
There is no loss at all until you sell

quiz.question: When you buy a stock, what are you actually buying?
choices: A tiny slice of a real company
A gift card to a store
quiz.explanation: When you buy a stock, you're buying a tiny slice of an actual, real business — not just a picture or a promise. Owning shares in a snack company, for example, means you truly own a small part of that company.

quiz.question: Can everyday people, not just experts, own stocks?
choices: Yes, including teens with a parent's help
No, only professional traders can
quiz.explanation: Yes — millions of ordinary people, including teenagers with a parent's help, own small pieces of companies through simple accounts. You don't need to be a finance expert or a grown-up genius to start investing.

quiz.question: A sneaker company sells way more shoes than last year. What might happen to its stock?
choices: It could rise, fall, or stay similar depending on expectations and other factors
It must become more valuable
quiz.explanation: Higher sales can be good news, but a stock does not automatically rise. Investors also consider profits, future expectations, competition, costs, and the price they are already paying.

quiz.question: What's a key difference between investing and gambling?
choices: Investing means owning a real part of a business, unlike a guess-based bet
There is no difference at all

quiz.question: Why do risk and reward usually go together in investing?
choices: Taking on some risk is part of how money can grow more over time
Taking risks never has any effect on growth
quiz.explanation: Risk and reward go together because taking on some chance of loss is part of what allows money to grow faster than it would sitting still. A savings account barely grows, but accepting some risk, like owning stock, opens the door to bigger gains over years.

slides.title: Why is time powerful in investing?
slides.text:
More time gives an investment more chances for growth to compound and more time to recover from some market declines. Time does not remove risk, but it can make short-term ups and downs less important for long-term goals.

Example: Money invested at age 12 can remain invested for decades before retirement.

slides.title: What is compound growth?
slides.text:
Compound growth means returns can be earned on both the original money and earlier returns. This creates a snowball effect over long periods.

Example: If $100 grows 10% to $110, another 10% gain would be $11, making $121. Real investment returns are not fixed like this each year.

slides.title: How are short-term and long-term goals different?
slides.text:
Money needed soon usually should not be exposed to large investment swings. Longer-term money has more time to handle temporary declines, although losses are still possible.

Example: Money for a game next month belongs in savings more than money for a goal 10 years away.

options.label: Yes, all money should be invested identically regardless of timeline
options.outcome: Money shouldn't be invested identically regardless of timeline — money needed soon usually should avoid large swings.

options.label: Timeline never matters for how money should be kept
options.outcome: Timeline actually matters a lot — money needed soon should generally avoid big investment swings.

slides.title: What does investing regularly mean?
slides.text:
Investing regularly means adding a set amount on a schedule, such as every month. This builds a habit and means you buy at many different prices instead of trying to guess one perfect day.

Example: Investing $10 each month buys more shares when prices are lower and fewer when prices are higher.

options.label: Investing regularly never actually changes anything

slides.title: How does compounding build over time?
slides.text:
Compounding becomes more noticeable as the total gets larger, because future gains can apply to previous gains too.

Example: At a hypothetical 8% yearly return, $200 becomes $216 after one year and about $233.28 after two. Actual returns vary and can be negative.

options.label: Compounding never actually builds over time
options.outcome: Compounding actually does build over time — that's exactly why the second year's gain was larger than the first.

slides.title: Can small amounts really matter?
slides.text:
Yes. Small amounts can become meaningful when they are added consistently over many years. The habit often matters more than starting with a large amount.

Example: $5 a week adds up to $260 of contributions in one year before any investment gain or loss.

options.outcome: Small amounts actually do add up — $5 a week adds up to $260 over a full year.

options.outcome: Small, consistent amounts can add up to something substantial, like $260 in a year, through the habit of saving regularly.

slides.title: Why does starting earlier give you an advantage?
slides.text:
Starting earlier gives each dollar more years to potentially compound. Someone who begins later can still build wealth, but may need to save more to reach the same goal.

Example: $500 invested at age 11 has many more years to grow than $500 first invested at age 25.

slides.title: How should a goal affect where money goes?
slides.text:
Your timeline matters. Money needed soon is usually kept in safer, easier-to-access places, while money for distant goals may be invested more aggressively.

Example: A phone in three months and college in ten years should not necessarily use the same type of account.

options.label: Timelines never affect where money should be kept

slides.title: Does regular investing remove market risk?
slides.text:
No. Regular investing can reduce the pressure to choose the perfect purchase date, but it cannot prevent losses or guarantee a profit.

Example: Investing $20 every month means buying across different prices, but the total value can still fall when markets decline.

options.outcome: Regular investing doesn't guarantee you'll never lose money — the total value can still fall when markets decline.

options.label: Regular investing removes all risk completely

quiz.question: Why is starting young such a big advantage for investing?
choices: More time for your money to grow
It isn't actually an advantage
quiz.explanation: Starting young matters because time lets compound growth do its work, turning small amounts into much larger ones. $100 invested at age 12 has decades to grow before retirement, far more than the same $100 invested at 40.

quiz.question: $100 growing 10% becomes $110. Why does year two's 10% growth apply to $110, not $100?
choices: Because that's compound interest — growth building on top of previous growth
Because banks round numbers up randomly

quiz.question: What is "dollar-cost averaging"?
choices: Investing a smaller amount regularly instead of all at once
Only ever investing in dollar bills
quiz.explanation: Dollar-cost averaging means investing a smaller, steady amount on a regular schedule, like $10 every month, instead of one big lump sum. This way, you naturally buy at both high and low prices, which smooths out the ride.

quiz.question: $200 grows at 8% a year. Why does year two's growth apply to $216, not $200?
choices: Because compounding builds on the new, larger total each year
Because banks add a random bonus each year
quiz.explanation: Compounding means each year's growth is calculated on the total you have so far, including previous growth. $200 becomes $216 after year one, and in year two the 8% growth applies to that bigger $216, not the original $200.

quiz.question: Investing $5 a week for a year adds up to about how much?
choices: About $260
About $26
quiz.explanation: $5 a week for 52 weeks adds up to about $260 — small, steady amounts build into a real total surprisingly fast. Left to grow for years afterward, that pattern can turn into an even bigger sum.

quiz.question: $500 invested at age 11 vs the same $500 invested at age 25 — which has more time to grow before retirement?

They have exactly the same amount of time

quiz.question: You want to buy a new phone in 3 months. Where should that money likely stay?
choices: In simple savings, not invested
Invested, since more time always helps
quiz.explanation: Money you'll need soon, like in 3 months for a phone, should stay in simple savings rather than invested. Investments can dip in value for a while, and a short-term dip could mean you don't have enough when you need it.

quiz.question: Why might investing the same amount every month help smooth out ups and downs?
choices: You end up buying more when prices are low and less when high
It guarantees prices never change

quiz.question: What is the biggest advantage a young investor typically has?

A bigger allowance than adults

slides.title: What is a brokerage account?
slides.text:
A brokerage account is an account used to buy, sell, and hold investments such as stocks, bonds, ETFs, and mutual funds. It is different from a bank savings account, which is mainly designed to hold cash.

Example: A parent might use a custodial brokerage account to buy an index fund for a child.

slides.title: What is diversification?
slides.text:
Diversification means spreading money across different investments so one bad result has less effect on the whole portfolio. It reduces some risks, but it does not eliminate all risk.

Example: A fund holding hundreds of companies is more diversified than owning only one company’s stock.

slides.title: What is inflation?
slides.text:
Inflation means the general price level rises over time, so each dollar may buy less than before. Inflation rates change from year to year.

Example: If a snack costs $2 today, it may cost more in the future even though it is the same snack.

options.label: Prices never change over time

slides.title: What is an index fund?
slides.text:
An index fund is a fund designed to follow a market index by owning many of the investments in that index. It can provide diversification in one purchase.

Example: An S&P 500 index fund holds shares in hundreds of large U.S. companies instead of just one.

slides.title: Why do investment fees matter?
slides.text:
Fees reduce the money that stays invested and can compound over time. Even a small yearly percentage can make a noticeable difference over many years.

Example: A 1% annual fee on $1,000 is about $10 in the first year; the long-term cost can be much larger as the account grows.

slides.title: What is a custodial account?

A custodial account is an account an adult manages for a minor. The assets belong to the child, but the custodian controls the account until the age set by law.

Example: A parent may buy investments in the account while the child learns how the account works.

options.label: Nobody owns the assets in this type of account

slides.title: What should you research before buying a stock?
slides.text:
Research means learning how a company makes money, whether it earns profits, how much debt it has, who its competitors are, and what risks it faces. No amount of research can guarantee a stock will rise.

Example: A popular product is only one clue; investors also look at the company’s financial health.

slides.title: Why can cash lose buying power?
slides.text:
Cash does not physically shrink, but inflation can reduce what the same number of dollars can buy. Interest on savings can help offset some of that loss in buying power.

Example: $20 may buy four items today but only three similar items years from now if prices rise enough.

options.label: Cash can never lose buying power

slides.title: How do you read a simple investment statement?

A statement shows what you own, how many shares you have, the current price, and the total value. It may also show deposits, withdrawals, dividends, and gains or losses.

Example: If you own 3 shares priced at $40 each, their current market value is $120.

quiz.question: What is a brokerage account used for?

Only storing cash, like a regular bank account
quiz.explanation: A brokerage account is specifically where you buy and hold investments like stocks, unlike a regular bank account that just holds cash. A parent might open one for a teen so they can pick companies to invest small amounts in, with supervision.

quiz.question: What does diversification mean?

Putting all your money in one company

quiz.question: What is inflation?

Prices always staying exactly the same
quiz.explanation: Inflation is prices slowly rising over time, which means money that just sits still buys a little less each year. A $1 snack rising 3% a year could cost about $1.16 after five years.

quiz.question: What is an index fund?

A type of piggy bank

quiz.question: What is a custodial account?
choices: A brokerage account a parent manages for a kid until they're an adult
A type of savings piggy bank
quiz.explanation: A custodial account is a brokerage account that a parent opens and manages for a kid until they become an adult. It lets a young person actually own real investments earlier than they otherwise could on their own.

quiz.question: Why do smart investors research a company before buying its stock?
choices: So they invest with real reasons instead of just guessing
Research never actually helps
quiz.explanation: Researching a company before buying its stock means looking into what it does, how it's been performing, and whether you believe in its future. This helps you invest with real reasons behind your choice instead of just guessing.

quiz.question: Why does keeping money as plain cash slowly lose value?
choices: Because inflation makes prices rise while the cash stays the same
Because cash actually shrinks in size over time
quiz.explanation: Cash kept under a mattress doesn't earn anything, but prices around it keep rising due to inflation. That means the same amount of cash buys a little less each year, even though the number of dollars never changes.

About $100

quiz.question: Why might an index fund be easier for a beginner than picking individual stocks?

It only ever invests in one company

slides.title: Why is diversification important?

Diversification spreads your money across different companies, industries, or asset types so one problem does not control your entire result. It lowers concentration risk, but a broad market decline can still affect many investments at once.

Example: Owning a broad index fund is generally more diversified than putting all $500 into one stock.

slides.title: What is an index fund?
slides.text:
An index fund aims to match the performance of a specific market index rather than picking investments one by one. Many index funds hold hundreds or thousands of securities and often have relatively low fees.

Example: A total-market index fund can give one investor exposure to a large part of the U.S. stock market.

slides.title: What is the Rule of 72?
slides.text:
The Rule of 72 is a shortcut for estimating how long money might take to double at a steady percentage return: divide 72 by the annual rate. It is only an estimate, and real investment returns change from year to year.

Example: At a hypothetical 8% return, 72 ÷ 8 is about 9 years.

slides.title: What is a bull market?
slides.text:
A bull market is a period when prices in a broad market have risen substantially, commonly described as a rise of about 20% or more from a recent low. The exact start and end are usually clearer after the fact.

Example: A long stretch of rising stock prices may be called a bull market.

slides.title: What is a bear market?
slides.text:
A bear market is commonly described as a decline of about 20% or more from a recent market high. Bear markets have historically been followed by recoveries, but the timing and size of any recovery are never guaranteed.

Example: A market index falling from 100 to 80 would represent a 20% decline.

slides.title: What is compound growth?
slides.text:
Compound growth means returns can generate additional returns over time. It can accelerate growth, but negative returns can also compound in the opposite direction.

Example: At a hypothetical 7% return, $1,000 becomes $1,070 after one year, and the next year’s return starts from the new value.

slides.title: How are stocks and bonds different?
slides.text:
Stocks represent ownership in a company. Bonds are debt: the investor lends money to a government or company in exchange for promised interest and repayment terms. Both can lose value and carry different risks.

Example: A company stock may rise with business growth, while a company bond may pay scheduled interest if the issuer can meet its obligations.

options.label: Stocks and bonds are exactly the same thing

slides.title: What is a portfolio?
slides.text:
A portfolio is the complete collection of investments a person owns. The mix of stocks, bonds, cash, and other assets is called asset allocation.

Example: One investor might hold stock funds, bond funds, and cash, with the percentages chosen to match their goals and risk level.

slides.title: What is volatility?
slides.text:
Volatility describes how much and how quickly an investment’s price moves up and down. High volatility means larger price swings, not automatically higher or lower long-term returns.

Example: A stock moving from $100 to $80 to $115 in a short period is more volatile than one staying near $100.

Spreading your money across many different investments

A market that only sells stuffed animals

Only earning money once at the very end

quiz.question: What's the main difference between a stock and a bond?

They are exactly the same investment

A single type of stock only

quiz.question: What is a bull market?

A market that only trades farm animals

Because it's required by law

Long-term investing focuses on goals measured in years rather than reacting to every market move. Frequent trading or panic selling can create costs, taxes, and poor timing, but simply holding an investment is not a guarantee of success.

slides.title: How does debt compound against you?

Debt charges interest on money you borrowed. If interest and fees are not paid, the balance can grow, meaning compounding can work against you rather than for you.

An emergency fund is money kept in a safe, accessible place for unexpected expenses. It can keep you from needing to sell investments or use high-interest debt at a bad time.

Debt is better judged by its cost, purpose, terms, and your ability to repay it than by a simple “good” or “bad” label. A low-cost education loan may support future earnings, while high-interest credit-card debt for nonessential purchases can be much harder to manage.

During a downturn, investment values can fall significantly and may take months or years to recover. Some investments never return to an earlier high, which is why diversification and an appropriate time horizon matter.

Example: $1,000 could fall to $700; from there it might recover, fall further, or move sideways.

slides.text:
Your time horizon is how long until you expect to need the money. Generally, a longer horizon allows more time to recover from market declines, while a shorter horizon calls for more stability.

Example: Money for tuition next year is usually treated differently from retirement money needed in 40 years.

options.label: No — a longer time horizon can typically handle more risk than money needed soon
options.outcome: Exactly! Your time horizon (how soon you'll need the money) affects how much risk makes sense — longer horizons can typically ride out more ups and downs.

options.label: Yes, time horizon doesn't matter at all
options.outcome: Time horizon matters a lot — money needed soon generally shouldn't be in the same risky investments as money you won't touch for decades.

options.label: Money needed soon should take on more risk
options.outcome: That's backwards — money needed soon generally should take on LESS risk, since there's less time to recover from a downturn.

quiz.question: A candy bar costs $1 today. If prices rise 3% a year, what happens to its price over 10 years?
choices: It rises to roughly $1.34, since prices rising over time is inflation
It always stays exactly $1
quiz.explanation: Prices rising over time is called inflation, and it means money that just sits still slowly loses buying power. A $1 candy bar rising 3% a year would cost roughly $1.34 after ten years, so the same dollar buys noticeably less.

quiz.question: True or False: Reacting quickly to every market dip usually leads to better long-term results.
choices: True
False
quiz.explanation: False — reacting to every dip by selling in a panic usually hurts long-term results more than it helps. Investors who stay patient through ups and downs over years or decades have historically ended up far ahead of those chasing quick moves.

quiz.question: A $200 credit card balance at 20% interest grows if unpaid. Why is this the "opposite" of investing?
choices: Because compounding is working against you instead of for you
Because credit cards use a completely different kind of math
quiz.explanation: A $200 credit card balance charging 20% interest can balloon if left unpaid, because interest compounds on top of interest, the same mechanism that grows investments — just working in the wrong direction. Debt grows against you while investing aims to grow money for you.

quiz.question: What is an emergency fund for?
choices: Cash you can use for surprises without selling your investments
Money you're never allowed to touch
quiz.explanation: An emergency fund is cash set aside for surprises, like a car repair, that you can reach without selling your investments. Keeping a few months of expenses in easy-to-reach savings means a sudden bill doesn't force you to sell at a bad time.

quiz.question: Why might a loan for education be viewed differently from debt for something that loses value fast?
choices: It can increase future earning power, though it still costs interest
Because it never has to be paid back
quiz.explanation: A loan for education is often viewed differently from debt for something that loses value fast, because it can increase your future earning power. Even so, it still costs extra through interest, so borrowing less is almost always the safer choice.

quiz.question: Someone spends $500 a month. Using a 3-to-6-month target, about how much might their emergency fund aim to hold?
quiz.explanation: A common emergency fund target is 3 to 6 months of expenses kept in easy-to-reach savings. Someone spending $500 a month would multiply that out to aim for somewhere between $1,500 and $3,000 before investing more aggressively.

quiz.question: An investment drops from $1,000 to $700, then recovers to $1,050 a year later. Who "locks in" the loss?
choices: Someone who panics and sells while it's at $700
Someone who waits it out
quiz.explanation: Someone who panics and sells while the investment is down at $700 locks in that loss permanently, turning a temporary dip into a real one. Someone who waits it out gets to keep the eventual recovery, ending up with $1,050 instead.

quiz.question: What does "time horizon" mean?
choices: How long until you'll actually need the money
How much money you currently have
quiz.explanation: Time horizon means how long until you'll actually need the money you've invested. Someone investing for a goal 15 years away can usually handle a much bigger dip than someone who needs the money in just six months.

quiz.question: Someone investing for a goal 15 years away can usually handle bigger dips than someone needing the money in 6 months. Why?
choices: They have much more time to wait out a recovery
Time horizon has no effect on risk
quiz.explanation: A longer time horizon gives an investment far more time to recover from a downturn before the money is actually needed. Someone with 15 years to go can simply wait out a rough stretch, while someone needing cash in 6 months can't afford to wait.

quiz.question: What is a retirement account generally used for?
choices: Investing money you won't touch for decades, often with tax benefits
Spending money the same week you earn it
quiz.explanation: A retirement account is built for investing money you won't touch for decades, often with tax benefits that help it grow faster. Some employers even add extra money when you contribute, like adding $25 for free when you put in $50.

slides.title: How can a teenager start learning to invest?
slides.text:
A teenager can begin by learning the basics, practicing with a mock portfolio, and—where allowed—investing with a parent or guardian through an appropriate custodial or youth account. Starting small helps build habits without pretending risk disappears.

Example: A teen might track a broad index fund for a few months before investing real money with an adult.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teen tracks a broad index fund for a few months before investing real money. What does this practice help with?

options.label: Building habits without pretending risk disappears
options.outcome: Exactly right! Starting small and practicing, like tracking a mock portfolio, helps build habits without pretending risk disappears.

options.label: Nothing — practicing has no real benefit
options.outcome: Practicing actually has real benefit — it helps build good habits before investing real money.

options.label: This guarantees they will not lose money later
options.outcome: Practicing doesn't guarantee against future losses — it helps build habits, but risk doesn't disappear.

slides.title: How can taxes affect investing?
slides.text:
Investment taxes depend on the account type, the kind of income, how long an investment was held, and local tax law. Selling for a profit may create a taxable capital gain, while some retirement accounts have special tax rules.

Example: Buying for $100 and selling for $150 creates a $50 gain before considering taxes or fees.

widgetConfig.scenario: You buy for $100 and sell for $150. What does this create, before considering taxes or fees?

options.label: A $50 capital gain
options.outcome: Exactly right! Selling for a profit, like buying at $100 and selling at $150, creates a $50 taxable capital gain before considering taxes or fees.

options.label: A $50 loss
options.outcome: This is actually a gain, not a loss — you sold for $50 more than you paid.

options.label: Taxes never apply to any investment activity
options.outcome: Taxes actually can apply to investment activity, like a capital gain from selling at a profit.

slides.title: Why do fees matter so much over time?
slides.text:
Investment fees reduce returns every year, and the money paid in fees also loses the chance to compound in the future. Comparing expense ratios and other costs is therefore important.

Example: A 1% annual fee on $10,000 starts around $100 per year, while a 0.05% fee starts around $5.

widgetConfig.scenario: Two similar funds have different fees: one charges 0.1% per year, the other 1.5% per year. Over 30 years, does this small-looking difference matter much?

options.label: Yes — small fee differences compound and can cost a huge amount over decades
options.outcome: Exactly! Fees might look tiny year to year, but compounded over decades, even a 1% difference can cost tens of thousands of dollars in lost growth.

options.label: No, such small percentage differences don't matter at all
options.outcome: They actually matter a lot over long periods — fee differences compound just like investment growth does, often adding up to a huge difference.

options.label: Fees only matter for the first year
options.outcome: Fees are charged every year, so their impact compounds over the entire time you're invested, not just the first year.

slides.title: What are risk tolerance and risk capacity?
slides.text:
Risk tolerance is how comfortable you feel with losses and volatility. Risk capacity is how much loss your financial situation and timeline can actually handle. They are related but not the same.

Example: You may feel comfortable with risk, but money needed for college next year may still have low risk capacity.

widgetConfig.scenario: You feel emotionally fine with risky investments (tolerance), but you need this money for rent next month (capacity). Which should guide your decision?

options.label: Risk capacity — your actual financial situation matters more than how you feel
options.outcome: Exactly — even if you're emotionally comfortable with risk, your real capacity (needing the money soon) should guide the decision. Risk capacity is about your actual circumstances.

options.label: Risk tolerance — just go with how you feel
options.outcome: Feeling comfortable with risk doesn't change the real consequences if you need that money soon — capacity matters more here.

options.label: Neither matters, just pick randomly
options.outcome: Both matter, but when money is needed soon, your actual capacity to handle a loss should guide the decision more than your comfort level.

slides.title: How does a custodial brokerage account work?
slides.text:
In a custodial brokerage account, an adult custodian manages investments for a minor. The assets belong to the minor, and control transfers at the age required by the account and state law.

Example: A parent can manage investments while a teen learns, but the money is not simply the parent’s personal account.

widgetConfig.scenario: A parent manages investments for a teen in this account. Whose money is it really?

options.label: The minor's — it is not simply the parent's personal account
options.outcome: Exactly right! In a custodial brokerage account, the assets belong to the minor, even though an adult custodian manages the investments.

options.label: The parent's personal money entirely
options.outcome: The money isn't the parent's personal money — the assets belong to the minor, even though the parent manages it.

options.label: Nobody really owns the money in this account
options.outcome: Someone does own the money in this account — specifically, it belongs to the minor.

slides.title: Why should investors keep records?
slides.text:
Records help track purchase price, sale price, dividends, fees, and taxes. Brokerages often provide statements and tax forms, but understanding your cost basis makes investment results easier to measure.

Example: If you bought 5 shares at $20 and later sold them at $28, your records help calculate the gain before taxes and fees.

widgetConfig.scenario: You bought 5 shares at $20 and sold them at $28. What do good records help you calculate?

options.label: The gain before taxes and fees
options.outcome: Exactly right! Records help track purchase price, sale price, and more — understanding your cost basis makes investment results easier to measure, like calculating this gain.

options.label: Nothing useful at all
options.outcome: Records actually are quite useful — they help you calculate gains, like the one from this sale, before taxes and fees.

options.label: Records are only needed if you lose money
options.outcome: Records are useful whether you gain or lose money — they help calculate results either way, like this gain.

slides.title: How do you compare fund fees?
slides.text:
Look at the expense ratio and any other trading or account costs. A small percentage difference can become meaningful when the balance is large or the investment is held for decades.

Example: On $5,000, a 1% yearly expense ratio is about $50, while 0.05% is about $2.50 before considering changes in account value.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're comparing two similar investment funds. What should you look at to compare their fees?

options.label: The expense ratio and other trading or account costs
options.outcome: Exactly! Comparing the expense ratio and any other costs tells you the real fee difference, which matters a lot over time.

options.label: Just whichever fund has a more exciting name
options.outcome: A fund's name tells you nothing about its cost — comparing the expense ratio and other fees is what matters.

options.label: Fees are all the same so there's nothing to compare
options.outcome: Fees actually vary a lot between funds — comparing the expense ratio and other costs reveals real differences.

slides.title: How should investments match your goals?
slides.text:
Investment choices should reflect the goal, time horizon, need for cash, ability to handle losses, and overall diversification. There is no single portfolio that fits everyone.

Example: Money for a house in five years may be invested more cautiously than retirement money needed in 40 years.

widgetConfig.scenario: Money for a house in five years versus retirement money needed in 40 years. Should these be invested the same way?

options.label: Not necessarily — goals, timeline, and risk tolerance matter
options.outcome: Exactly right! Investment choices should reflect the goal, time horizon, need for cash, and ability to handle losses — there is no single portfolio that fits everyone.

options.label: Yes, there is one single portfolio that fits everyone
options.outcome: There isn't one single portfolio that fits everyone — goals and timelines, like five years versus forty, call for different approaches.

options.label: Time horizon never affects how money should be invested
options.outcome: Time horizon actually affects this a lot — a five-year goal and a forty-year goal usually call for different approaches.

slides.title: Why should you avoid investing money you need soon?
slides.text:
Short-term money can be hurt by bad timing. If the market falls just before a bill is due, you may have to sell at a loss.

Example: Tuition due in six months is usually better kept somewhere stable and accessible than in a volatile stock fund.

widgetConfig.scenario: Tuition is due in six months. Where is this money usually better kept?

options.label: Somewhere stable and accessible, not a volatile stock fund
options.outcome: Exactly right! Short-term money can be hurt by bad timing — tuition due in six months is usually better kept somewhere stable and accessible.

options.label: In the most volatile investment available
options.outcome: A volatile investment is risky for money needed soon — if the market falls right before the bill is due, you might have to sell at a loss.

options.label: It does not matter where short-term money is kept
options.outcome: It actually matters a lot where short-term money is kept — a volatile investment risks a loss right when you need the money.

quiz.question: What's one key benefit of starting to invest as a teenager instead of waiting until your 30s?
choices: Many more years for compound growth
No real benefit either way
quiz.explanation: Starting to invest as a teenager instead of waiting until your 30s gives your money many more years for compound growth to work. A small amount invested at 16 has decades longer to grow than the same amount invested at 32, even without adding more.

quiz.question: You buy a stock for $100 and sell it for $150. What might a capital gains tax apply to?
choices: The $50 profit you made
The full $150 you received
quiz.explanation: A capital gains tax typically applies only to the profit made from selling an investment, not the full amount received. If you bought a stock for $100 and sold it for $150, the tax would generally apply to the $50 profit, not the whole $150.

quiz.question: What is an expense ratio?
choices: A small yearly fee some investments charge
A tax on all your income
quiz.explanation: An expense ratio is a small yearly fee some investments charge just for holding them, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A $10,000 investment with a 1% expense ratio costs about $100 a year, which can add up to thousands over a few decades.

quiz.question: In a custodial brokerage account, who legally controls it until the teen reaches a set age?
choices: A parent
A random stranger
quiz.explanation: A parent legally controls a custodial brokerage account, even though the investments inside it actually belong to the teen. At a set age, often 18 or 21 depending on the state, full control transfers over to the teen.

quiz.question: Why is it smart to keep simple records of what you paid and sold an investment for?
choices: It makes figuring out any tax owed on the profit much easier
Records are never actually needed
quiz.explanation: Keeping simple records of what you paid for an investment and what you sold it for makes it far easier to figure out any tax owed on the profit. A quick note of dates and prices at the time saves a lot of hassle later on.

quiz.question: Fund A charges 0.05% a year and Fund B charges 1%. On a $5,000 investment, roughly what's the fee gap in one year?
choices: About $47.50 more for Fund B
There is no real difference
quiz.explanation: Fund A's 0.05% fee costs about $2.50 a year on $5,000, while Fund B's 1% fee costs about $50, a gap of roughly $47.50 in just that one year. Over decades, small fee differences like this compound into a much larger gap.

quiz.question: Why might someone saving for a house in 5 years choose steadier investments than someone saving for retirement in 40 years?
choices: They have less time to recover from a big dip
Steadier investments are always required by law
quiz.explanation: Someone saving for a house in 5 years has much less time to recover from a big dip than someone investing for retirement 40 years away. A shorter time horizon leaves less room to ride out a downturn before the money is actually needed.

quiz.question: Why is it risky to invest money you'll need within the next year or two?
choices: A bad month could force you to sell at a loss to cover a bill
Investing that money always guarantees a profit
quiz.explanation: Investing money you'll need within the next year or two is risky because a bad month in the market could force you to sell at a loss just to cover a bill. Keeping short-term money out of investments protects it from that kind of bad timing.

quiz.question: What does risk tolerance mean?
choices: How comfortable you are watching your investment's value swing up and down
How much money you're required to invest
quiz.explanation: Risk tolerance describes how comfortable you are watching your investment's value swing up and down without panicking and selling. Someone investing money they won't need for 20 years can usually handle bigger swings than someone who needs the money in just one year.

quiz.question: What's one benefit modern investing apps and custodial accounts give a teenager?
choices: An easier way to start investing small, real amounts with a parent's help
Guaranteed profits with no risk at all
quiz.explanation: Modern investing apps and custodial accounts make it far easier for a teenager to start investing small, real amounts with a parent's help. A 16-year-old could begin with just $20 in an index fund and add a bit more each month from there.
